questions.question: Given the English sentences “All detectives are clever.” and “John is a detective.”, convert them into first‑order predicate logic Horn clauses and determine using resolution refutation whether the query “John is clever.” is entailed.

options.A: Yes, the query is entailed after resolution.
options.B: No, the query is not entailed because the KB is incomplete.
options.C: The query is both entailed and contradicted.
options.D: Resolution cannot be applied to this set of clauses.

questions.explanation:
“All detectives are clever” → ∀x (Detective(x) ⇒ Clever(x)) which is a Horn clause (conjunction ⇒ symbol). “John is a detective” → Detective(John). Adding ¬Clever(John) to the KB and converting to CNF yields a resolvable contradiction, showing KB ⊨ Clever(John) (unsatisfiable KB ∧ ¬Clever(John)) [Page 180].

questions.question: Convert the sentences “If someone is a programmer then they are logical.” and “Alice is a programmer.” into Horn clauses, then using resolution refutation decide whether the query “Alice is logical.” holds.

options.B: The query is not entailed because the rule is not in Horn form.
options.C: The query is false under the KB.
options.D: Resolution yields a non‑Horn clause, so the query cannot be decided.

questions.explanation:
“If someone is a programmer then they are logical” → ∀x (Programmer(x) ⇒ Logical(x)), a Horn clause. “Alice is a programmer” → Programmer(Alice). Adding ¬Logical(Alice) leads to a resolvent that contradicts the KB, proving entailment [Page 185].

questions.question: The knowledge base contains the Horn clauses: (1) ∀x (Bird(x) ⇒ CanFly(x)), (2) ∀x (Penguin(x) ⇒ Bird(x)), (3) Penguin(Tweety). Convert to clause form and use resolution refutation to answer the query “CanFly(Tweety)”.

options.B: The query is not entailed because of an implicit exception.
options.C: The query is both entailed and refuted.
options.D: Resolution cannot derive a conclusion due to missing facts.

questions.explanation:
After Skolemization and CNF, the clauses are ¬Bird(x) ∨ CanFly(x), ¬Penguin(x) ∨ Bird(x), Penguin(Tweety). Adding ¬CanFly(Tweety) resolves to a contradiction, showing KB ⊨ CanFly(Tweety) [Page 180].

questions.question: Translate the statements “Every robot that has sensors is autonomous.” and “R2D2 has sensors.” into Horn clauses. Using resolution refutation, determine whether the query “R2D2 is autonomous.” is a logical consequence.

options.A: Yes, the query follows from the KB.
options.B: No, the KB does not guarantee autonomy.
options.C: The query is undecidable with resolution alone.
options.D: The conversion produces a non‑Horn clause, so resolution is inapplicable.

questions.explanation:
“Every robot that has sensors is autonomous” → ∀x (Robot(x) ∧ Sensors(x) ⇒ Autonomous(x)), a Horn clause. “R2D2 has sensors” and “R2D2 is a robot” (assumed) give premises; adding ¬Autonomous(R2D2) leads to a resolvent that empties, proving entailment [Page 185].

questions.question: From the sentences “If a student studies then the student passes.” and “Mia studies.”, form the corresponding Horn clauses and apply resolution refutation to decide the truth of the query “Mia passes.”.

options.A: The query is entailed by the KB.
options.B: The query is not entailed because the rule is missing a premise.
options.C: The query is both true and false under different models.
options.D: Resolution fails because the KB is not in CNF.

questions.explanation: “If a student studies then the student passes” → ∀x (Studies(x) ⇒ Passes(x)), a Horn clause. “Mia studies” → Studies(Mia). Adding ¬Passes(Mia) yields a resolvent that contradicts the KB, so KB ⊨ Passes(Mia) [Page 180].
